variants.title: Trace the proxied request
variants.context: One reverse-proxy request crosses four boundaries in order: negotiate and bound the connection while preserving a request ID and deadline; match host, port, path, and method; serve a cache entry or choose an upstream with connect, send, read, retry, and buffering policy; return the result while recording edge time, upstream time, cache status, and the selected upstream.
variants.prompt: A browser requests /api/orders through NGINX. Put the edge steps in order.

items.text: Match host, port, path, and method against location rules.
Negotiate TLS and HTTP, bound header and body size, and preserve a request ID and deadline.
Serve an eligible cache entry or choose an upstream and apply timeouts, retry, and buffering policy.
Return status, headers, and body while recording edge time, upstream time, cache status, and the selected upstream.

variants.hint: Routing happens before any upstream connection.
variants.explanation: Connect → route → serve or proxy → return with evidence. Every arrow is a contract boundary that must stay observable.

variants.title: Trace the proxied request
variants.context: One reverse-proxy request crosses four boundaries in order: negotiate and bound the connection while preserving a request ID and deadline; match host, port, path, and method; serve a cache entry or choose an upstream with connect, send, read, retry, and buffering policy; return the result while recording edge time, upstream time, cache status, and the selected upstream.
variants.prompt: A request hits a cached response. Put the steps in order, including where it ends.

items.text: Return the response and record the cache status as a hit.
Negotiate the connection and bound the request.
Match the location rule that enables caching.
Serve the cache entry under its identity and freshness policy without contacting the origin.

variants.hint: A hit ends before any upstream attempt.
variants.explanation: Cache identity must include everything that changes the response, or one tenant can receive another’s page.

variants.title: Trace the proxied request
variants.context: One reverse-proxy request crosses four boundaries in order: negotiate and bound the connection while preserving a request ID and deadline; match host, port, path, and method; serve a cache entry or choose an upstream with connect, send, read, retry, and buffering policy; return the result while recording edge time, upstream time, cache status, and the selected upstream.
variants.prompt: The upstream times out. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Location matched and an upstream selected.
A controlled error is returned and the attempt result is recorded; no automatic retry of a mutation.
Connection negotiated and bounded with a deadline.
The read timeout fires; the upstream result is unknown.

variants.hint: A timeout is not proof the upstream did nothing.
variants.explanation: Retrying a POST after a proxy timeout can repeat the mutation; make retry policy match the application contract.

variants.title: Name the role
variants.context: NGINX can be a web server (respond locally), a reverse proxy (forward intentionally with deadlines and buffering), a load balancer (distribute across upstreams), and an HTTP cache (serve a hit or permitted stale response). Name each role separately.
variants.prompt: NGINX serves a health endpoint and static assets without opening any upstream connection. Which role is that?
options: Web server.
Reverse proxy.
Load balancer.
optionFeedback: Responding locally is the web-server role.
A proxy forwards to an upstream.
Balancing chooses among upstreams.
variants.hint: Did the request leave the edge?
variants.explanation: Name each responsibility separately so its authority and failure behavior stay reviewable.

variants.title: Name the role
variants.context: NGINX can be a web server (respond locally), a reverse proxy (forward intentionally with deadlines and buffering), a load balancer (distribute across upstreams), and an HTTP cache (serve a hit or permitted stale response). Name each role separately.
variants.prompt: NGINX normalizes the request boundary, applies deadlines and buffering, and forwards to one application. Which role?
options: HTTP cache.
Web server.
Reverse proxy.
optionFeedback: A cache avoids source work; this request reaches the upstream.
The edge is not answering from local files.
Forwarding intentionally with policy is the reverse-proxy role.
variants.hint: Is the request forwarded with policy?
variants.explanation: A reverse proxy gives a system one controlled boundary in front of its services.

variants.title: Name the role
variants.context: NGINX can be a web server (respond locally), a reverse proxy (forward intentionally with deadlines and buffering), a load balancer (distribute across upstreams), and an HTTP cache (serve a hit or permitted stale response). Name each role separately.
variants.prompt: NGINX stores reusable responses under an explicit identity and serves a permitted stale response during an outage. Which role?
options: Load balancer.
Reverse proxy only.
HTTP cache.
optionFeedback: Balancing does not store responses.
A plain proxy would fail with the upstream.
Serving a hit or permitted stale response is the cache role.
variants.explanation: Stale-if-error is a cache policy decision with product consequences.

variants.title: Count the sockets
variants.context: worker_connections limits the connections one worker can own, including upstream connections. A proxied request occupies a client socket and an upstream socket at the same time. It is not a requests-per-second setting.
variants.prompt: Four workers each allow 4,096 connections. Every proxied request holds one client socket and one upstream socket. Roughly how many proxied requests can be in flight at once?
variants.hint: Total connection slots divided by sockets per request.
variants.explanation: 4 × 4,096 = 16,384 slots; two sockets per request gives about 8,192 concurrent proxied requests.

mistakes.feedback: Each proxied request holds two sockets.

variants.title: Count the sockets
variants.context: worker_connections limits the connections one worker can own, including upstream connections. A proxied request occupies a client socket and an upstream socket at the same time. It is not a requests-per-second setting.
variants.prompt: Eight workers each allow 2,048 connections, and each request holds two sockets. How many concurrent proxied requests fit?

mistakes.feedback: Divide by the two sockets each request holds.

variants.title: Count the sockets
variants.context: worker_connections limits the connections one worker can own, including upstream connections. A proxied request occupies a client socket and an upstream socket at the same time. It is not a requests-per-second setting.
variants.prompt: The edge has 8,192 connection slots in total and 10,000 idle keep-alive client connections arrive. How many cannot be held?
variants.explanation: 10,000 − 8,192 = 1,808 connections have no slot. Keep-alive, HTTP/2, and slow clients change the concurrency shape.

mistakes.feedback: That is the capacity, not the shortfall.

variants.title: Pick the method
variants.context: No balancing method knows application capacity automatically: round robin is a baseline for similar servers, least connections helps with long or uneven requests, hash routing gives stable affinity, weights encode mixed capacity.
variants.prompt: Six identical instances serve requests of similar cost. Which method is the sensible baseline?
options: Hash routing.
Least connections.
Round robin.
optionFeedback: Affinity is unnecessary here.
Connection count adds little for uniform requests.
Rotation is a clear baseline when instances and costs are similar.
variants.hint: Are the servers and requests similar?
variants.explanation: Start with the baseline; add a signal only when the workload needs it.

variants.title: Pick the method
variants.context: No balancing method knows application capacity automatically: round robin is a baseline for similar servers, least connections helps with long or uneven requests, hash routing gives stable affinity, weights encode mixed capacity.
variants.prompt: Requests vary from 10 ms to 30 seconds. Which method helps most, and what is its limit?
options: Round robin, since request duration averages out over time.
Weights, because they encode how much each server can take.
Least connections; connection count is still a proxy for load.
optionFeedback: Rotation ignores duration, so a 30 second request still lands on a busy server.
Weights encode capacity differences, not live load.
Long, uneven requests pile up on a round-robin target; connection count reacts to that.
variants.hint: What signal reflects a long request still running?
variants.explanation: Connection count approximates work; it can still be misleading for multiplexed connections.

variants.title: Pick the method
variants.context: No balancing method knows application capacity automatically: round robin is a baseline for similar servers, least connections helps with long or uneven requests, hash routing gives stable affinity, weights encode mixed capacity.
variants.prompt: A cache-heavy service wants the same key to land on the same server. Which method, and what must be planned?
options: Hash routing on the affinity key, with a plan for membership change.
Round robin with sticky session cookies pinning each client to a server.
Least connections across the whole upstream group.
optionFeedback: Stable affinity needs a declared key and a plan for membership change.
Cookies pin sessions but do not keep cache keys together.
Least connections balances load and ignores which key a request carries.
variants.hint: What happens to affinity when a server leaves?
variants.explanation: Choose the key from the real affinity boundary and plan remapping.

variants.title: Keep routing safe
variants.context: Routing must be explicit: one owner per host and path, admin and status locations unreachable from untrusted networks, a deliberate Host value, tested configuration before reload. A proxy timeout leaves the upstream result unknown, and a retry can repeat a mutation.
variants.prompt: An upstream receives the proxy’s own hostname in Host and misroutes the request. What is wrong?
options: The proxy does not pass the original Host; set it deliberately.
The upstream is broken and should ignore the Host header.
TLS is missing, so the upstream cannot see the real host.
optionFeedback: Pass a deliberate Host value.
The upstream is doing what the header says.
TLS does not change Host.
variants.hint: Which header did the upstream trust?
variants.explanation: Make routing behavior explicit and test it before reload.

variants.title: Keep routing safe
variants.context: Routing must be explicit: one owner per host and path, admin and status locations unreachable from untrusted networks, a deliberate Host value, tested configuration before reload. A proxy timeout leaves the upstream result unknown, and a retry can repeat a mutation.
variants.prompt: The /status and admin locations are reachable from the internet. What is the fix?
options: Make the admin and status locations unreachable from the internet.
Rename them to obscure paths that nobody outside the team knows about.
Add a longer timeout so scanners give up on them.
optionFeedback: Restrict by network and identity; exact locations must not be shadowed by prefix rules.
A renamed path is still public, and nothing stops the request.
A timeout changes how long a request waits, not who may make it.
variants.explanation: Test exact and prefix locations so sensitive handlers are not exposed.

variants.title: Keep routing safe
variants.context: Routing must be explicit: one owner per host and path, admin and status locations unreachable from untrusted networks, a deliberate Host value, tested configuration before reload. A proxy timeout leaves the upstream result unknown, and a retry can repeat a mutation.
variants.prompt: proxy_read_timeout fires on a POST that creates an order. Should NGINX retry the next upstream?
options: Yes, retry once against the next upstream in the group.
No. The result is unknown, so a retry can create a second order.
Yes; a read timeout means the upstream never got the request.
optionFeedback: One retry is one chance at a duplicate order; the count is not the issue.
Retry only where the application contract allows it.
A read timeout only says no response arrived; the order may already exist.
variants.hint: What does the upstream know that the proxy does not?
variants.explanation: Start from the end-to-end request contract, then configure NGINX to preserve it.
